name: immutability
intent: Make shared data unchangeable after it is created, so every logical update produces a new version that can be published, cached and read concurrently without defensive copies, locks or invalidation, while unchanged parts of a structure are shared between versions.
problem: Shared mutable data hands control to every holder: any component, thread or pipeline stage can change what all the others see, so callers copy data in and out defensively, caches and keys go stale, and concurrent readers need locks that mostly arbitrate reads. The recurring decision is whether a piece of shared data gets a single owner with controlled mutation, or is modelled as a sequence of immutable versions that readers may keep forever.
context: Applies to data that is read by many and written by few - configuration and routing tables, cached derivations, event payloads, model state in a UI or functional pipeline - and to any data crossing threads, components or trust boundaries where the alternative is locking or defensive copying. It pays off when updates can be expressed as producing the next version, and it is cheap when the language or its ecosystem offers persistent collections, copy-on-write value types, or a type system that distinguishes shared from exclusive access.
benefits: Readers need no coordination: a version that cannot change can be shared across threads, requests and modules without locks, and the only remaining care is publishing the reference safely.
No defensive copies at boundaries: code can hand out references to its data instead of copying it in and out, which removes a whole class of aliasing bugs and the copy-in/copy-out boilerplate.
Caching and memoization become sound: content-derived equality and hashing cannot change under the key, so values can be interned, memoized, diffed and compared cheaply by reference or by content.

Every change is an explicit new value, so history is free: previous versions stay valid for undo, audit and time travel, and a failing computation can keep a reference to the exact state that produced it.

Structural sharing keeps versioning affordable: persistent collections copy only the path to the change and share the rest, so the cost of an update is logarithmic in the structure rather than a deep copy.
Consistent snapshots are published by swapping one reference: a writer builds the next version off to the side, so readers never observe a half-updated structure.
tradeoffs: Allocation pressure: every logical update creates at least one new version, so update-heavy loops that were free in place now allocate; structural sharing, transients/builders, or mutating values that are provably unique are the mitigations.
Nested updates get verbose: changing one field deep inside a structure becomes a chain of copy-with calls or needs an optics/lens layer, and that ergonomic cost is paid at every call site.
Retention inverts the memory story: shared nodes keep old versions alive, so one long-lived root can pin a large part of the history, turning a GC problem into an explicit retention policy.
Shallow guarantees fail silently: freeze, readonly, final, and unmodifiable markers protect one level, and a getter or field that exposes mutable interior state voids the guarantee without any error.

Equality and hashing become obligations: values used as keys must define content equality, and one mutable or array-typed component breaks it - unhashable values, reference equality, or stale map entries.

Interop friction and unenforceable discipline: ORMs, serializers and mutable APIs expect setters, and in languages without enforcement (C, Go, JavaScript, TypeScript) the guarantee rests on review - a single in-place write to a shared version breaks every reader.

participants.responsibility: The value or collection that is created fully formed and never modified afterwards: the unit that any number of readers may hold without copying or locking.
A pure function that derives the next version from a version plus an input and returns it as a new value; it must never write to the structure it reads.
The representation that makes those updates affordable: path copying or structural sharing lets versions share unchanged nodes instead of deep-copying the whole structure.
The single mutable cell that names the current version - a variable, an atomic pointer, a store key; swapping it is the only mutation in the system.
A mutable accumulator confined to one update operation or batch that is frozen into an immutable value when the batch ends.
Any consumer of a version; it may hold the reference indefinitely because the data cannot change under it, and it never needs to copy or lock.

use_cases: Configuration, routing and registry tables swapped atomically: one writer publishes a new immutable snapshot while readers keep using their loaded version until they reload.
Event, command and message payloads on a pipeline: a fact published to several consumers must not be editable by one of them.
Caches and memoization keyed by value: derivation results, interned constants and compiled rules stay valid because their keys cannot change.
Application state in a redux-style or functional flow, where the store holds one immutable state tree and every action produces the next version.
Undo, history and auditing: editors, versioned documents and temporal data keep previous versions referenced instead of copying state at every step.
Lock-free sharing between threads, tasks or worker pools: workers read a published immutable snapshot while a single writer prepares the next one.
Event sourcing and audit logs: append-only immutable event sequences are replayed to reconstruct state, giving free history, temporal queries and time-travel debugging without any special mechanism.

Frontend state management (React/Redux pattern): a single immutable state tree is held in a store; every action returns a new version, enabling time-travel debugging, hot reloading, and deterministic replay.
Append-only ledger and blockchain patterns: financial or data-integrity systems that require a tamper-evident history use immutable blocks or entries that are never modified after commit.
Read-model projections in CQRS architectures: query-side read models are built as immutable projections of immutable events; they are replaced wholesale when a projection is rebuilt.
Feature flag and experiment configurations: a flag's state snapshot is immutable once published, so every evaluation sees a consistent configuration regardless of concurrent rollouts.
ML model versioning and artifact stores: trained model artifacts and their metadata are stored immutably; lineage, reproducibility and rollback depend on no version being altered after upload.

Clojure's persistent vectors, hash-maps and hash-sets: use transient/persistent! scopes to batch construction while publishing only the final immutable value, preserving safe sharing without paying for every intermediate version.

Immutable.js v5 List, Map and Set collections: nested setIn/updateIn operations return persistent values with structural sharing, value equality and memoization-friendly change detection for JavaScript state.

Erlang/OTP's persistent_term storage: publish read-heavy configuration or runtime constants as immutable Erlang terms for lock-free constant-time reads, while treating replacement as an exceptional write path.
avoid_when: The data is provably single-owner and hot: mutate the local buffer, counter or array in place (Rust &mut, a Go local, a JavaScript accumulator); versioning uniquely owned data is pure overhead.
Large binary buffers and streaming data: bytes are copied, not structurally shared - keep the buffer mutable and confined, or transfer ownership.
Bulk construction or accumulation: use a mutable builder/transient/StringBuilder and freeze once at the boundary instead of folding thousands of versions.
A framework owns the data and requires mutation (ORM entities, JavaBeans, editor models): map to immutable values at the edge and keep mutability outside, or do not apply the pattern there at all.
Updates vastly outnumber reads and the structure is deep: measure first - in-place mutation under a single owner often beats path copying.
anti_patterns: Immutability by convention: the type is documented as immutable but some internal path still writes to shared state in place.
Shallow freeze presented as the guarantee: a frozen object whose nested arrays and objects remain mutable, or an unmodifiable view over a collection that another component keeps writing.
Deep-copying everything on every update instead of sharing structure or using a transient, which replaces the mutation cost with a worse copy cost and hides the real bottleneck.
Version churn on uniquely owned hot data: folding a loop into thousands of throwaway immutable versions where a single mutable accumulator was intended.
Treating a read-only view as a copy: wrapping a collection in an unmodifiable/frozen view and then mutating the original, invalidating the guarantee for every holder of the view.
design_principles: Referential transparency: an update depends only on its inputs, never on hidden mutable state, so equal inputs give equal results.
Separation of shared from exclusive access: data is shared as immutable versions, and mutation is confined to the single handle that publishes the next version.
Value semantics: equality, hashing and identity of what is shared follow from content, so sharing can never change meaning.
Design by contract with construction-time validation: invariants hold for a version's whole life and are checked once, when it is built.
Explicit state transitions: every change is a named function producing a new version, so the history of changes is itself a first-class value.
best_practices: Build values fully formed in one factory or constructor that validates its inputs and copies or freezes what it stores, then never expose a reference through which the state could change.
Return new versions from update functions (withX/copy/plus/map) and never write to the version you were given.

Prefer persistent collections with structural sharing - path copying, tries, cons lists, copy-on-write buffers - over deep copies for large nested data, and use a transient or builder for batches that are frozen once.
Keep exactly one mutable handle to the current version (variable, atomic pointer, store key) and publish new versions by swapping it atomically.
Make equality and hash follow content for anything used as a key, and prefer immutable field types (tuple/frozenset/ImmutableArray) so hashing cannot break later.
Use freeze/readonly/unmodifiable markers at trust and module boundaries to catch accidental writes, and prefer types that are immutable by construction over markers on mutable ones.

Use one-shot freeze or builder patterns for complex construction: accumulate mutable state in a builder or transient, then freeze exactly once at the boundary, rather than building immutably step by step.

Keep immutable types focused on a single responsibility: each value object should model one concept; composed larger objects are built by combining focused immutable values rather than packing everything into one large immutable class.
Design immutable types to be serializable and deserializable without breaking guarantees: use the same canonical form on the wire as in memory, and validate all constraints again on deserialization.

Document equality semantics explicitly: state whether the type uses value-based (content) equality and what that means for collections containing mutable keys, so clients can predict behavior without guessing.

Use immutable DTOs and message contracts at microservice and module boundaries: in/out objects crossing a trust boundary must not alias internal mutable state; they should be immutable by construction rather than convention.
Combine with event sourcing for audit trails: immutability of past events is a prerequisite for reliable history; each new state version is a derived projection of an immutable event sequence.

Prefer types that are immutable by construction over types merely marked as immutable: algebraic data types, record types, and final classes with only final fields give stronger guarantees than freeze or readonly annotations that can be bypassed.
sources: Okasaki, C., Purely Functional Data Structures (Cambridge University Press, 1998) - persistence, structural sharing and path copying for data structures that never change.
Bloch, J., Effective Java, 3rd ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2018), Item 17 Minimize mutability - immutable classes and copy-with construction instead of setters.

Goetz, B., Peierls, T., Bloch, J., Bowbeer, J., Holmes, D. & Lea, D., Java Concurrency in Practice (Addison-Wesley, 2006), Chapter 3 Sharing Objects - immutable objects are always thread-safe and are published safely through final fields.
Henney, K., Immutable Value (workshopped at PLoP 98) - https://c2.com/ppr/wiki/JavaIdioms/ImmutableValue.html

Hickey, R., The Value of Values (JaxConf 2012, InfoQ, 2012) - https://www.infoq.com/presentations/Value-Values/ — compares value-oriented vs place-oriented programming; immutability enables simpler reasoning and better concurrency in distributed systems.

GeeksforGeeks, Immutable Architecture Pattern - System Design (2024) - https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/system-design/immutable-architecture-pattern-system-design/ — immutable architecture best practices including event sourcing and domain-driven value objects.

Microsoft Learn, Azure Architecture Center, Event Sourcing Pattern (2024) - https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/event-sourcing — Azure's canonical description: immutable event log as source of truth, state derived by replaying events.

Richardson, C., Pattern: Event Sourcing (Microservices.io, 2024) - https://microservices.io/patterns/data/event-sourcing.html — links event sourcing to CQRS, saga and transaction logs; immutability underpins the event store.

Bach, E., Distributed Microservices with Event Sourcing and CQRS (Medium, 2022) - https://medium.com/@bacheric/distributed-microservices-with-event-sourcing-and-cqrs-fc11497c4378 — immutable events as the write model; read projections replaced wholesale on rebuild.

Wikipedia, Algebraic Data Type (2024) - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_data_type — ADTs (sum types, product types, discriminated unions) pair with immutability: an immutable sum type makes invalid states structurally unrepresentable.

Driscoll, Sleator, Tarjan & Thurston, Making Data Structures Persistent - http://www.cs.cmu.edu/~sleator/papers/another-persistence.pdf — formalizes partial and full persistence and efficient version sharing.
Clojure Reference, Transient Data Structures - https://www.clojure.org/reference/transients — official guidance for scoped transient mutation followed by persistent publication.
Immutable.js Documentation v5 - https://immutable-js.com/docs/v5/ — official persistent immutable List, Map, Set and nested-update APIs for JavaScript.
Erlang/OTP, persistent_term - https://erlang.org/documentation/doc-16-rc3/erts-16.0/doc/html/persistent_term.html — official read-optimized immutable-term storage and its costly update/GC behavior.

Bolívar Puente, Persistence for the Masses: RRB-Vectors in a Systems Language - https://public.sinusoid.es/misc/immer/immer-icfp17-preprint-00.pdf — evaluates cache, memory-management and transient tradeoffs for immutable persistent vectors.
